system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Linearizability
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: The consistency condition requiring concurrent executions to match a sequential execution that respects real-time operation order. Covers handling of incomplete operations, linearization points, composability, and the contrast with sequential consistency. Excludes proofs for specific implementations.

ATOMS:
- CS-DIST-C07-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: An implementation of an object is linearizable if, for any complete concurrent execution of the object, there is a sequential execution with the same operations and return values whose total order of operations is a linearization of the partial order of operations in the concurrent execution.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0171-s14] The strongest consistency property generally used is lineariz- ability [HW90], which says roughly that an implementation of an object is linearizable if, for any complete concurrent execution of the object, there is a sequential execution of the object with the same operations and return values, where the (total) order of operations in the sequential execution is a linearization of the (partial) order of operations in the concurrent execution.
- CS-DIST-C07-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: The partial order $<_H$ on operations in a concurrent execution $H$ is defined by $a <_H b$ when the response event of operation $a$ precedes the invoke event of operation $b$ in $H$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0171-s15] The order in each case is deﬁned as a <H b if the response event for opera- tion a in execution H precedes the invoke event for operation b in the same execution.
- CS-DIST-C07-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: A linearization of an execution requires a sequential execution $S$ that meets the object's sequential specification, satisfies $H''|p = S|p$ for every process $p$, and satisfies $<_{H''} \subseteq <_S$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0172-s09] Construct a sequential S such that S meets the sequential speciﬁcation of the object, H′′|p = S|p for all p, and <H′′⊆<S.2
- CS-DIST-C07-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: Linearizability can alternatively be shown by assigning each operation a linearization point between its invocation and response. The sequential execution $S$ is then obtained by treating every operation as occurring atomically at its linearization point, consistent with the object's specification.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0172-s15] An alternative method is to assign each operation a linearization point somewhere between when its invocation and response, and obtain S by assuming that all operations occur atomically at their linearization points is consistent with the speciﬁcation of the object; this is equivalent to constructing <S⊇<H since given <S we can always ﬁnd consistent linearization points.
- CS-DIST-C07-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: Linearizability is composable: if $H|A$ is linearizable for each object $A$, then $H$ is linearizable.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0173-s08] Linearizability has the useful property of being composable, in the sense that if H|A is linearizable for any particular object A, then H is linearizable.
- CS-DIST-C07-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: A linearization of a possibly incomplete concurrent execution $H$ is built in three steps: - Extend $H$ with zero or more response events to get $H'$. - Remove the invoke events in $H'$ that have no matching response to get $H''$. - Construct a sequential execution $S$ that meets the object's sequential specification, with $H''|p = S|p$ for all processes $p$ and $<_{H''} \subseteq <_S$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0172-s03] implementation the ﬂexibility of deciding whether these operations have taken eﬀect or not, so given an incomplete concurrent execution H, a linearization of H involves three steps:
    [CS-DIST-p0172-s05] Extend H by adding zero or more response events, obtaining a new execution H′.
    [CS-DIST-p0172-s07] Remove any invoke events in H′ that don’t have a matching response event, obtaining a new execution H′′.
    [CS-DIST-p0172-s09] Construct a sequential S such that S meets the sequential speciﬁcation of the object, H′′|p = S|p for all p, and <H′′⊆<S.2
- CS-DIST-C07-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: Sequential consistency is weaker than linearizability: it requires only a sequential execution indistinguishable to all processes, essentially dropping the requirement $<_H \subseteq <_S$. That sequential execution may therefore order operations differently from the global order.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0173-s05] This says that for any concurrent execution of the object, there exists some sequential execution that is indistinguishable to all processes; however, this sequential execution might include operations that occur out of order from a global perspective.
    [CS-DIST-p0173-s06] (Essentially we are dropping the requirement <H⊆<S from the linearizability deﬁnition.) For example, we could have an execution of an atomic register where you write to it, then I read from it, but I get the initial value that precedes your write.
- CS-DIST-C07-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: Linearizability of an implementation can usually be proved using only complete executions when the implementation guarantees that any operation in progress can eventually finish. In that case any incomplete $H$ can be extended to a complete $H' = H''$ by running pending operations to completion.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0172-s13] Even better, if we are asking if an implementation of an object is linearizable—meaning that all executions of the object are linearizable—then we can usually prove this by proving it only for complete executions, since if the implementation has the property that any operation in progress can eventually ﬁnish, we can extend any incomplete H to a complete H′ = H′′ by simply running any pending operations to completion.
- CS-DIST-C07-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: Sequential consistency does not generally have the composability property that linearizability has.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0173-s09] Sequential consistency does not generally have this property.
